scenario: AITA for offending a friend after she rejected help she asked for? | Hello! I'll try to be brief. Friend (28F) let's call her *Jade* was spoiled financially from age 12 to 18 by father and developed habits of eating out, eating premade stuff, never cooked, best brands of candy every day. At 18 dad cut her off (he and the mother are divorced), and now for past 10 years she's struggling with meeting ends working part time jobs. This year it hit really hard since her government-welfare ended. Now, she, her mom, and her brother (18M) are living from mom's 300 eur salary. Jade by being really picky with food is actually starving. She claims that she needs about 7 euros per meal that she would eat. She refuses to cook and now, they don't even have a stove to cook on, just microvawe. Me (24F) I grew up in a bit more financially responsible family and we barely eat out, we cook at home and usually bring meals to work, ect. Despite meeting ends well, I manage to make a "price" of meal about 2-3 euros. It is simple but healthy food, usually rice or buckwheat + some meat, eggs, bread, vegetables. It doesn't even get that repetetive for me even though the meals do look absolutely basic. Well, Jade, being my friend for 11 years, has been opening up and complaining lately, a lot. She actually is starving. She said lack of chocolate drives her crazy, and that she barely eats anything at all because mother doesn't give her money to eat (and she doesn't like to eat what mom buys). She asked for help. I offered dark chocolate since we have a lot at home. *Rejected.* I offered to cook to her rice, buckwheat, eggs, give her vegetables, fruit, bread. *Rejected.* I kept offering help and she said I'm offering her food that she "doesn't like" and if I want to help I should give her cash. I do want to help her, but not in cash, since she would spend it in 2 days what I could make food for 1 week with the same amount. I was offering healthy stuff that I eat myself, but it is not good enough to her. Well, I snapped and said "let me know when poverty and starvation lowers your standards". AITA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I did the right thing or not in this situation with my friend Jade. Let me start by understanding the background. Jade has had a pretty privileged upbringing financially, but things changed when her dad cut her off at 18. Now, she's struggling financially, living with her mom and brother, and they're barely making ends meet. She's really picky about her food, which is causing her to not eat properly, and she's even starving because she refuses to eat what her mom buys or prepare her own meals. I, on the other hand, grew up in a more financially responsible family. We don't eat out much, and we cook at home, bringing meals to work. I manage to keep my meals simple but healthy, costing about 2-3 euros per meal. I offered to help Jade by giving her dark chocolate and cooking her some basic meals, but she rejected both offers. She wants cash instead, which I'm hesitant to give because I think she'll spend it in a day or two on things that aren't necessary, like more expensive food or treats. In the end, I snapped and told her, "Let me know when poverty and starvation lower your standards." Now, I'm wondering if I did the right thing or not. Was it appropriate for me to say that, or was it offensive? First, I need to consider why I reacted that way. I was probably feeling frustrated because I wanted to help her, but she wasn't accepting the help I was offering. I thought my way of providing food was better for her because it's healthier and more sustainable. But she didn't see it that way. She wanted cash so she could buy what she wanted, even if it wasn't as healthy or sustainable. I also need to think about our friendship. We've been friends for 11 years, so I know her pretty well. She's always been picky about food, so maybe this isn't a new issue. But now, with her financial struggles, it's become more critical because she's not eating properly. I was trying to help, but my approach might have come off as judgmental or dismissive of her feelings. Another thing to consider is the cultural or personal context. Maybe in her upbringing, she was always given the best, so now she's struggling to adjust to a more modest lifestyle. It's hard to change habits, especially when it comes to something as personal as food. She might feel like she's losing a part of herself or her identity by having to eat differently. I also need to reflect on my own feelings. I was trying to help, but I felt like my efforts were being rejected. It's frustrating when you want to assist someone, but they don't accept your help in the way you're offering it. Maybe I should have communicated differently or found another way to support her that aligns with her preferences. Perhaps I should have had a conversation with her about why she's rejecting the food I'm offering. Understanding her perspective might have helped me find a better way to assist her. Instead, I snapped, which might have made her feel worse or more defensive. I also need to think about the long-term consequences of my actions. If I continue to offer help in a way that she doesn't appreciate, it might strain our friendship. On the other hand, if I don't help her, she might continue to struggle with her food issues, which could have negative health impacts. Maybe there's a middle ground. Instead of offering to cook for her, I could have suggested grocery shopping together so she can pick out some healthier options that she likes. Or maybe I could have offered to teach her how to cook simple, affordable meals that she might enjoy more than what I was offering. I also need to consider her emotional state. She's going through a tough time financially, and that can take a toll on your mental health. She might be feeling stressed, anxious, or even depressed, which could be contributing to her pickiness about food and refusal to eat what's available. Maybe she needs emotional support more than anything else, and my focus on providing food wasn't addressing her deeper needs. In the future, I should think about how to approach similar situations more effectively. Communication is key. Instead of getting frustrated and snapping, I could have expressed my concerns more calmly and asked her what she really needs. Active listening would have helped me understand her perspective better and find a solution that works for both of us. I also need to reflect on whether I have the capacity to help her in the way she wants. If giving her cash isn't feasible for me because I don't want her to spend it irresponsibly, maybe there are other ways to support her financially or emotionally. Perhaps I could have suggested setting up a budget together or finding ways to stretch her money further. Overall, I think my intention was goodâĢĶI wanted to help my friend. But my approach might have been too rigid and didn't take into account her feelings and preferences. In the future, I should be more mindful of how I offer help and ensure that it's something she's willing to accept and that it addresses her actual needs.
